title: AI application evals: prerequisite research graph
reader_assumptions: Basic Python, functions, records, loops and API calls are familiar.
No machine-learning, evaluation or AI-engineering background.
The support assistant’s policies, tool privileges and deployment details are unspecified; examples must remain hypothetical.
edge_semantics: A -> B means B requires A, not chronology or topical association.

nodes.question: What can the reader already do?
nodes.answer: Read records, call a function or API, compare values, and repeat work in a loop.

nodes.question: What exactly are we evaluating?
nodes.answer: The application behavior produced by its prompt, model, and other components for a particular use case, rather than a model’s general benchmark ranking.

nodes.question: Why does one successful answer not establish reliability?
nodes.answer: Generative outputs can vary even for the same input, and future inputs can differ from the few examples tried.

nodes.question: What would acceptable support behavior mean?
nodes.answer: Write observable requirements grounded in the company’s policy and intended support task. Correctness, useful responses and handling unsupported requests need explicit expectations.

nodes.question: What inputs should the test contain?
nodes.answer: A reusable dataset should cover real tasks, common cases, unusual inputs, and known failures; logs, experts and synthetic cases can supply candidates.

evidence.locator: What are evals?; Types of evals; How to read evals; Evals tips; Design your eval process
evidence.claim: Examples should represent use cases, failures and unusual inputs.

nodes.question: How do we know what should have happened in each case?
nodes.answer: Store expert judgments or reference information with the input; this expresses intended behavior rather than treating any generated answer as truth.

evidence.locator: Create a dataset; What annotation does; Annotation starting points; Incorporate expert annotations; Add graders
evidence.claim: References and expert annotations record intended behavior.

nodes.question: What happens during one evaluation run?
nodes.answer: For each saved case, run the configured application, save its output, then assess that output against the case’s criteria. Save the configuration so subsequent runs can be interpreted.

evidence.locator: Create an eval for a task; Test a prompt with your eval > Uploading test data; Creating an eval run; Analyze the results
evidence.claim: A run combines test data and generation configuration, producing outputs and grades.
evidence.access: Supplied verified paraphrase packet; original page not opened in this run

nodes.question: How does an output become a result?
nodes.answer: A grader receives the test information and response and returns a judgment. Exact matching suits fixed categories; qualitative responses need criteria that allow acceptable alternative wording.

evidence.locator: Overview; String check graders; Text similarity graders; Model graders > Score model graders; Python graders
evidence.claim: Different grader types measure distinct properties; exact matching can reject equivalent wording.
evidence.access: Supplied verified paraphrase packet; original page not opened in this run

nodes.question: Why must automated grades themselves be checked?
nodes.answer: A convenient measurement can reward behavior unlike the quality we want. Compare automated judgments with informed human judgments and inspect disagreements.

evidence.locator: What are evals?; Types of evals; How to read evals; Evals tips; Design your eval process
evidence.claim: Check automated assessments against human assessments.
evidence.access: Supplied verified paraphrase packet; original page not opened in this run

nodes.question: How do we evaluate actions and conversations, not just one answer?
nodes.answer: A support assistant may need evaluation of multiple turns and actual tool outcomes rather than only the wording of its last response.

nodes.question: What does a score mean?
nodes.answer: A score summarizes the measured behavior on the sampled cases. A generic metric or unrepresentative dataset may misstate production usefulness.

evidence.locator: What are evals?; Types of evals; How to read evals; Evals tips; Design your eval process
evidence.claim: Scores are evidence about measured behavior, not unrestricted claims of quality.
evidence.access: Supplied verified paraphrase packet; original page not opened in this run

nodes.question: How do we compare changes without overinterpreting scores?
nodes.answer: Rerun reusable examples and graders after a change and inspect improvements and regressions. Repeated runs, close-score uncertainty, and held-out cases need further evidence.

evidence.locator: Create a dataset; What annotation does; Annotation starting points; Incorporate expert annotations; Add graders
evidence.claim: The same data and graders support repeatable prompt or model comparisons.
evidence.access: Supplied verified paraphrase packet; original page not opened in this run

nodes.question: How does testing guide improvements?
nodes.answer: Inspect individual failures, revise the responsible component, rerun evaluations, and turn discovered real failures into reusable cases.

evidence.locator: What are evals?; Types of evals; How to read evals; Evals tips; Design your eval process
evidence.claim: Capture failures and rerun after component changes to reveal gains and regressions.
evidence.access: Supplied verified paraphrase packet; original page not opened in this run

nodes.question: What is a small first support-assistant eval?
nodes.answer: Choose one support task, annotate representative examples, run the assistant and grade its behavior, inspect results with a support expert, then change one component and rerun.

nodes.question: Why do I need AI application evals, how do they work, and how do I start evaluating a customer-support assistant?
nodes.answer: Evals turn explicit expectations and reusable cases into evidence about application behavior. They support improvements when the cases and grading rules reflect the support task; initial support workflow and comparison limits require further research.

edges.why: An evaluation loop is composed of familiar records, API calls and stored outputs.
Acceptable behavior must be defined for the application being evaluated.
Case expectations must express the task’s intended behavior.
The task determines which situations a dataset must cover.
The run needs saved inputs to exercise the application.
The configuration identifies which application produced the outputs.
Judgments need the relevant expectations for each case.
A grader requires the actual output from the application.
To judge whether automation measures quality, first understand its rule.
The system boundary determines whether actions and turns are part of behavior.
Expected outcomes determine what action or conversation evidence is needed.
A numerical summary inherits the meaning of its individual judgments.
The sampled situations limit what the summary represents.
A score is meaningful only to the extent that grading tracks intent.
Comparing numbers requires knowing what they measure.
Output variability can affect differences between runs.
Evidence of gain and regression is needed to assess a proposed improvement.
A realistic support test must account for conversations and effects when present.
A starter workflow should close the loop from failures to evaluated changes.
The target explicitly asks how to begin.
Variation explains why informal spot checking is insufficient.
Knowing what scores establish explains the value and limits of evals.

gaps: Concrete support criteria and policy references
Multi-turn conversations and actual tool effects
Variability, held-out data and close-score interpretation
evidence: Supplied ai-evals.json: four official documentation paraphrases
